scenario: AITA in relation to my GF's attempt to lose weight? | I've been dating my GF for 3 years. She's upset at her current weight. She's put on about 100lbs since we started dating. I've never mentioned it because she has bipolar disorder, and as I struggle with depression I fully understand how food can take the edge off when you get seriously overwhelmed with depression. But for health reasons and of course other reasons, of course I would like for her to get back to a healthy weight. My girlfriend's bipolar disorder has been a challenge for me, as where I would normally be assertive in a relationship on issues - I often have to back down in arguments because she responds poorly to being challenged. I often feel like I'm walking on ice, but I do my best to try understand her and work at helping her and supporting her as best I can. She is not happy with her current weight, and constantly remarks about it and has been complaining about it for over a year without doing anything about it. I tell her we can work on it together as a team, and both fix our diet. I feel this is the best way to go about it, rather than telling her that SHE needs to lose weight. I don't want her feeling like I'm initiating it, or that it's a journey she needs to take alone. Or that I'm pushing her to do it. For it to be a healthy journey, it needs to be something she is motivated to do and if I do it with her, then it doesn't feel like it's all on her. So, last week she decided to work on her diet. She was upset today because she hasn't lost any weight yet. I told her to not worry about the short term results - that it had only been a week, but to focus on months down the line to see changes. She was extremely defeatist and said she'll never lose weight. This kinda irritated me, because it had only been a week since she started. I felt like she hadn't fully committed, because she was drinking soft drinks and eating chips which are high in carbs so I brought that up, if she wants to see results quicker - that cutting out the junk food completely (rather than cutting down) will help her. Now I understand she's trying to make a change, but the defeatist attitude after only a week is difficult to work with. She then got angry at me and told me to "stop arguing with me about my weight". To which I replied that I wasn't, I had never in our entire relationship brought up her weight, and was just discussing her diet and how she was eating and drinking things that will make her progress slower. She then told me to drop it and leave it alone, and is now in a huff with me for the past few hours over it. I understand this is the nature of her bipolar disorder, and she will shut down anything she's challenged about something. Am I the asshole for challenging her defeatist attitude on her results, when she was taking short-cuts with junk food?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I'm the asshole in this situation with my girlfriend. Let me start by understanding the scenario. We've been dating for three years, and she's been struggling with her weight, gaining about 100 pounds since we started dating. I know she has bipolar disorder, and I struggle with depression myself, so I understand how food can be a coping mechanism when you're overwhelmed. I've never mentioned her weight because I don't want to hurt her or trigger her condition. However, I do want her to be healthy, both for her well-being and for us as a couple. She's unhappy with her weight and has been talking about it for over a year but hasn't taken any real steps to change. I suggested that we work on our diet together as a team, which I thought was a good approach because it makes it a joint effort rather than something she has to do alone. I didn't want her to feel like I was pushing her or that it was her responsibility alone. Last week, she decided to start working on her diet. But today, she was upset because she hasn't lost any weight yet. I tried to reassure her that it's only been a week and that she should focus on the long-term changes. She became very defeatist, saying she'll never lose weight. That frustrated me because I felt like she wasn't fully committed, especially since she was still drinking sodas and eating chips, which are high in carbs. I brought that up, suggesting that cutting out junk food completely could help her see quicker results. She got angry, telling me to stop arguing about her weight. I explained that I wasn't bringing up her weight but was just discussing her diet and how her choices were slowing her progress. She told me to drop it and leave it alone, and now she's upset with me for the past few hours. I know her bipolar disorder makes her sensitive to being challenged, so I try to be careful. But I'm wondering if I overstepped by challenging her defeatist attitude, especially when she was taking shortcuts with junk food. So, am I the asshole here? Let me break it down. First, I didn't mention her weight directly, which I think is good because that could have been hurtful. Instead, I focused on her diet and the choices she was making. That seems reasonable because I was trying to support her in making healthier choices. However, she became upset when I pointed out that her choices were slowing her progress. She felt like I was arguing about her weight, even though I framed it as a discussion about diet. Maybe I should have been more gentle or not brought it up at all, considering her sensitivity. On the other hand, I was trying to help her by pointing out ways she could improve her results. I didn't want her to get discouraged so early in the process. But perhaps my approach was too direct, and I should have been more supportive without pointing out her shortcomings. I also need to consider her mental health. Bipolar disorder can make it hard for her to handle criticism or feel challenged, so my attempt to help might have come across as pushy or critical, even if that wasn't my intention. In the end, I think I might have been too direct in my approach. While my intentions were good, I should have been more sensitive to her feelings and perhaps found a different way to encourage her without making her feel criticized. Maybe I should have focused more on positive reinforcement and less on pointing out what she was doing wrong. So, considering all this, I think I might have been the asshole in this situation by being too direct and not considering her sensitivity enough. I should have approached the conversation more gently and focused on support rather than criticism.
